variants.title: Run the curation program
variants.context: Demonstration curation runs in four stages: specify the behavior contract, collect candidates with lineage, review and balance the accepted set, then evaluate a trained candidate and release a versioned artifact with a rollback target.
variants.prompt: A team is starting a demonstration dataset for a new assistant capability. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Review and balance: validate correctness and safety, remove duplicates, resolve disagreement, and fill measured coverage gaps.
Collect with lineage: capture source, authoring method, consent, license, tool use, and generator lineage per candidate.
Specify the behavior: write the rubric, refusal boundary, coverage matrix, and release gates.
Evaluate and release: train a pinned candidate, evaluate held-out slices, freeze the manifest, and keep a rollback target.

variants.hint: A reviewer cannot judge an example until something else exists.
variants.explanation: The behavior contract comes first because acceptance, coverage, and release gates all depend on a rubric a reviewer can apply consistently.

variants.title: Run the curation program
variants.context: Demonstration curation runs in four stages: specify the behavior contract, collect candidates with lineage, review and balance the accepted set, then evaluate a trained candidate and release a versioned artifact with a rollback target.
variants.prompt: Production escalations show the model refuses valid non-English requests. Put the feedback cycle in order.

items.text: Collect targeted candidates from the source best able to give independent evidence for that gap.
Convert the observed failure into an owned behavior, coverage, and risk requirement in the gap backlog.
Monitor production outcomes and record the refusal regression without treating raw user data as reusable training material.
Run the dataset gates, train a pinned candidate, replay held-out slices, and promote or roll back.
Apply the current rubric, preserve disagreement, and adjudicate the policy-sensitive cases.

variants.hint: An observed failure has to become an owned requirement before anyone collects for it.
variants.explanation: Curation operates as a feedback system, so a production gap becomes a backlog requirement before it becomes a collection order.

variants.title: Run the curation program
variants.context: Demonstration curation runs in four stages: specify the behavior contract, collect candidates with lineage, review and balance the accepted set, then evaluate a trained candidate and release a versioned artifact with a rollback target.
variants.prompt: A privacy incident is found in an already released dataset. Put the degraded path in order.

items.text: Keep serving the previous model and dataset bundle while the incident is investigated.
Quarantine the affected source and remove the affected record clusters.
Rebuild the derived splits, retrain, and repeat the held-out evaluation.
Stop promotion of the candidate release even though aggregate model quality improved.
Preserve the incident evidence without exposing sensitive content in routine logs or dashboards.

variants.hint: The first move protects users, not the dataset.
variants.explanation: A blocking gate failure stops promotion regardless of aggregate lift, and the previous bundle keeps serving while removal and retraining run.

variants.title: Build a review system that can disagree
variants.context: A review system is built to disagree. Deterministic checks run first, model-assisted checks route likely defects without establishing truth, qualified reviewers judge under the rubric, conflicts go to a named adjudicator, and clustered disagreement sends the rubric back for recalibration.
variants.prompt: A batch of 8,000 candidates arrives for review. Put the review stages in order.

items.text: Send conflicts and policy-sensitive cases to adjudication with a named owner.
Recalibrate the rubric when disagreement clusters around the same instruction or slice.
Use model-assisted checks to route likely defects rather than to settle truth silently.
Run deterministic checks for schema, empty fields, secret patterns, impossible metadata, and exact duplicates.
Assign qualified reviewers using blinded or overlapping review where disagreement matters.

variants.hint: Which check can be settled from the record alone, with no judgment at all?
variants.explanation: Cheap deterministic evidence runs first and model assistance only routes work, so scarce human judgment lands where the rubric is actually contested.

variants.title: Build a review system that can disagree
variants.context: A review system is built to disagree. Deterministic checks run first, model-assisted checks route likely defects without establishing truth, qualified reviewers judge under the rubric, conflicts go to a named adjudicator, and clustered disagreement sends the rubric back for recalibration.
variants.prompt: Two qualified reviewers give a high-consequence medical example opposite rubric scores. Put the handling in order.

items.text: Escalate the conflict to adjudication with a named owner rather than taking the majority.
Record the adjudicated outcome and the reason alongside the original disagreement.
Check whether the same disagreement is clustering on that instruction or slice.
Update the rubric guidance when the disagreement turns out to be systematic.
Record both dimension scores with reviewer qualification, confidence, and rubric version.

variants.hint: Disagreement is evidence to keep, not noise to average away.
variants.explanation: Preserving disagreement and adjudication is what turns a repeated conflict into a rubric fix instead of an arbitrary label.

variants.title: Build a review system that can disagree
variants.context: A review system is built to disagree. Deterministic checks run first, model-assisted checks route likely defects without establishing truth, qualified reviewers judge under the rubric, conflicts go to a named adjudicator, and clustered disagreement sends the rubric back for recalibration.
variants.prompt: A synthetic candidate enters the pipeline and eventually ships in a release. Put the evidence stages in order.

items.text: Review by a qualified human, recording rubric version, dimension scores, edits, and whether a human wrote, edited, or only viewed it.
Publish a manifest listing record hashes, exclusions, aggregate evidence, approvers, and rollback lineage.
Freeze the accepted content hash, transformations, coverage labels, split assignment, and links to prior versions.
Store the candidate with its input, target output, generator lineage, prompt, consent, and license.
Screen automatically for schema, secrets, duplicates, policy indicators, language, and benchmark overlap.

variants.hint: Each boundary appends evidence; no stage may erase the source.
variants.explanation: Synthetic outputs are candidates rather than independent truth, so generator lineage travels with the row all the way into the manifest.

variants.title: Size the review budget
variants.context: Two estimates size a curation program: candidate pool equals target accepted examples divided by the acceptance rate, and expert review hours equal candidate pool times the audit share times minutes per review, divided by 60.
variants.prompt: A program targets 9,000 accepted examples at a 60 percent acceptance rate, and plans to expert-audit 20 percent of the candidate pool at 6 minutes per review. How many expert hours does the audit consume?
variants.hint: The audit share applies to the candidate pool, not to the accepted target.
variants.explanation: Sizing runs from accepted target to candidate pool to review hours, which is what makes the operational load visible before a pilot starts.

mistakes.feedback: The 9,000 accepted target was used as the pool; rejected candidates are reviewed too.
That is the answer in minutes; the formula divides by 60.

variants.title: Size the review budget
variants.context: Two estimates size a curation program: candidate pool equals target accepted examples divided by the acceptance rate, and expert review hours equal candidate pool times the audit share times minutes per review, divided by 60.
variants.prompt: A pilot collects 24,000 candidates and audits 25 percent of them at 8 minutes per review. How many expert hours does that require?
variants.hint: Only the audited share of the pool costs review time.
variants.explanation: Expert hours are candidate pool times audit share times minutes per review divided by 60, so the audit share is the lever that changes the bill.

mistakes.feedback: Every candidate was charged review time; only 25 percent are audited.
That is the total in minutes rather than hours.

variants.title: Size the review budget
variants.context: Two estimates size a curation program: candidate pool equals target accepted examples divided by the acceptance rate, and expert review hours equal candidate pool times the audit share times minutes per review, divided by 60.
variants.prompt: A team has 240 expert hours available, audits 30 percent of candidates, and spends 5 minutes per review. How large a candidate pool can that budget support?
variants.hint: Convert the budget into reviews first, then undo the audit share.
variants.explanation: Running the sizing formula backwards turns a fixed review budget into the pool it can actually cover, which is how collection targets get bounded.

mistakes.feedback: That is the number of reviews the budget buys, not the pool those reviews sample from.
The 5 minutes per review was never applied to the budget.

variants.title: Name the curation failure
variants.context: Four curation failures recur: reward hacking the rubric, where surface patterns score well without the behavior; the synthetic feedback loop, where one model generates, scores, and filters its own patterns; coverage theater, where marginals look balanced but critical intersections are empty; and unrecoverable lineage.
variants.prompt: A postmortem lists four ways demonstration programs go wrong. Match each failure to its description.

pairs.label: Reward hacking the rubric
pairs.detail: Contributors learn surface patterns that score well without satisfying the intended behavior.

pairs.label: Synthetic feedback loop
pairs.detail: One model generates, scores, and filters its own patterns until its errors look consistent.

pairs.label: Coverage theater
pairs.detail: Marginal totals look balanced while critical slice intersections stay empty.

pairs.label: Unrecoverable lineage
pairs.detail: Licensed, private, or deleted material cannot be identified after training.

variants.hint: Two of these are failures of evidence and two are failures of measurement or governance.
variants.explanation: Naming the failure decides the fix, because rotating gold tasks, adding external evidence, gating intersections, and hashing lineage are not interchangeable.

variants.title: Name the curation failure
variants.context: Four curation failures recur: reward hacking the rubric, where surface patterns score well without the behavior; the synthetic feedback loop, where one model generates, scores, and filters its own patterns; coverage theater, where marginals look balanced but critical intersections are empty; and unrecoverable lineage.
variants.prompt: Four symptoms appear in one review cycle. Match each symptom to the failure it signals.

pairs.label: Contributor rubric scores keep rising while held-out model behavior stays flat
Language and difficulty totals look balanced but difficult non-English refusals has zero rows
Every generated variation shares one prompt template and repeats the same blind spot
After training, nobody can say which shards carried the licensed archive

variants.hint: Ask what evidence each symptom proves is missing.
variants.explanation: Symptoms point at different missing evidence, so each one calls for a different control rather than more rows.

variants.title: Name the curation failure
variants.context: Four curation failures recur: reward hacking the rubric, where surface patterns score well without the behavior; the synthetic feedback loop, where one model generates, scores, and filters its own patterns; coverage theater, where marginals look balanced but critical intersections are empty; and unrecoverable lineage.
variants.prompt: A second cycle raises four more symptoms. Match each to the failure it signals.

pairs.label: Reviewers approve answers that satisfy every rubric checkbox but miss what the user asked for
A deletion request arrives and the derived splits and checkpoints cannot be traced back
A judge model, a rubric model, and the generator all share one lineage
The matrix published with the release reports only one-dimensional totals

variants.hint: One symptom is about a rule being satisfied without being met; another is about a rule that was never gated.
variants.explanation: Shared lineage across generation, scoring, and judging removes the independence that evaluation depends on, which is a different failure from an ungated coverage matrix.

variants.title: Protect the effective sample size
variants.context: Row count is not teaching signal. Near-duplicate paraphrases, dominant templates, and repeated generators inflate the set while leaving effective sample size and behavioral coverage roughly unchanged.
variants.prompt: A team paraphrases 400 seed instructions into 10,000 rows. Row count rises 25 times, held-out evaluation stays flat. What is the diagnosis?
options: The dataset is still too small and needs another large paraphrase expansion.
The added rows are near-duplicates, so effective sample size barely moved.
The rubric is miscalibrated and the reviewers accepted incorrect targets.
optionFeedback: More paraphrases of the same 400 instructions repeat the signal that is already there.
Near-duplicate rows add count without adding independent teaching signal, which is exactly a flat evaluation.
Nothing here points at correctness; the accepted rows are consistent with the seeds they came from.
variants.hint: Ask how many independent behaviors the set actually demonstrates.
variants.explanation: Effective sample size is tracked through cluster concentration, unique source count, template share, and semantic-neighbor density, not row count.

variants.title: Protect the effective sample size
variants.context: Row count is not teaching signal. Near-duplicate paraphrases, dominant templates, and repeated generators inflate the set while leaving effective sample size and behavioral coverage roughly unchanged.
variants.prompt: Semantic clustering finds 60 nearly identical rows that all teach the same required refusal wording for a regulated request. What should happen?
options: Inspect the cluster, keep the convention, and cap its share if it crowds out rarer evidence.
Keep all 60 rows, since each one was individually reviewed and accepted.
Delete all but one automatically, since the cluster is a near-duplicate group.
optionFeedback: Clusters are inspected before deletion, and a dominant template is capped rather than erased.
Keeping every copy lets one template crowd out the rarer evidence the coverage matrix still needs.
Automatic deletion removes a valid repeated convention the behavior contract actually requires.
variants.hint: Ask whether this repetition is redundancy or a required convention.
variants.explanation: Duplicate removal is a judgment about evidence, so clusters are inspected first and dominant templates are capped rather than deleted wholesale.

variants.title: Protect the effective sample size
variants.context: Row count is not teaching signal. Near-duplicate paraphrases, dominant templates, and repeated generators inflate the set while leaving effective sample size and behavioral coverage roughly unchanged.
variants.prompt: One generator supplies 70 percent of accepted rows in a domain, and its rows pass every automated check. What is the right response?
options: Accept the concentration, because the generator passes the existing quality gates.
Cap the generator share so its repetition stops crowding out rarer evidence.
Remove every synthetic row from the domain and rebuild it from expert authoring.
optionFeedback: Passing gates measures each row alone and says nothing about the concentration across rows.
Capping dominant generators, templates, authors, and domains is how rarer evidence keeps its place in the set.
Removing all synthetic rows discards useful breadth when the problem is concentration, not the source.
variants.hint: Ask what the set loses when most of it comes from one place.
variants.explanation: Concentration caps on generators, templates, authors, and domains preserve independent evidence that per-row quality checks cannot see.
